title: Sponge thickness and hardness: what the numbers mean
seo_title: Rubber sponge thickness and hardness explained
description: What the sponge thickness and hardness numbers on a table tennis rubber mean, how they change speed, weight and control, and which to choose.
summary: Every rubber comes with a thickness in millimetres and often a hardness in degrees. Here is what the numbers measure, why brands differ and which to pick.
key_points: Thickness is the depth of the sponge under the top sheet; thicker sponge is heavier and gives more bounce.
Thickness labels are bands: Butterfly's 2.1 covers sponge between 1.9mm and 2.2mm.
"OX" means no sponge at all, and "max" means the maker's thickest, which varies from brand to brand.
Harder sponge needs a faster swing; Butterfly rates soft sponge as suited to beginners and hard sponge to advanced players.
Hardness scales are set by each maker, so a number from one brand cannot be compared directly with another's.
body: Most rubbers are a top sheet of pimpled rubber on a layer of sponge, and the two numbers on the packet describe that sponge. Thickness, in millimetres, is how deep the sponge is. Hardness, in degrees or points, is how firm it is. As a rule, thicker and harder sponge plays faster and suits strong attacking strokes, while thinner and softer sponge is slower, lighter and easier to control. Beginners should start thin and soft.
## What the rules allow

Under the ITTF Laws for 2026, a sponge rubber (sandwich rubber in the rules) must be less than 4.05mm thick in total, including the glue, and the pimpled top sheet may be no more than 2mm. Only one layer of sponge is allowed. The top sheet and the glue count towards that limit, so the sponge itself is always well under 4mm.
## Thickness: what the label means

The thickness printed on a rubber is a nominal size, not an exact measurement. Butterfly publishes the ranges behind its labels: a rubber sold as 2.1 has sponge between 1.9mm and 2.2mm, 1.9 means 1.7mm to 1.9mm, 1.7 means 1.5mm to 1.7mm and 1.5 means 1.3mm to 1.5mm. Its thinnest sponged category, 0.5, covers 0.4mm to 0.7mm.

Butterfly's own chart sets out what changes as sponge gets thicker. The rubber gets heavier, it gives the ball more bounce, and it moves from suiting defensive play to suiting offensive play. Less bounce means a slower ball that is easier to keep on the table while you learn. Our guide to [what bat to buy](/guide/what-table-tennis-bat-to-buy.html) gives a starting thickness.

Rubbers for attacking play are made in a narrow band of sizes. Butterfly's Tenergy 05 is made in 2.1, 1.9 and 1.7; its Dignics 09C only in 2.1 and 1.9. Defensive rubbers go much thinner: the long-pimpled Feint Long III comes in 1.3, 1.1 and 0.5, as well as with no sponge.
## "OX" and "max"

Two labels need explaining. "OX" means a rubber with no sponge at all: just the pimpled top sheet, glued straight to the blade. Butterfly makes it only in pimples-out and long-pimpled rubbers, where it gives a light, low-bounce covering. Butterfly sells its Feint Long III OX with an adhesive sheet already attached.

"Max" (sometimes "MX") means the thickest sponge a maker offers for that rubber. It is not a fixed measurement and differs between brands and even between rubbers, so check the figure in millimetres. The DHS Neo Hurricane 3 Hard, a Chinese rubber, is sold in a single 2.15mm thickness, for example, while Butterfly's thickest standard option on Tenergy 05 is 2.1.
## Hardness: what it changes

Hardness describes how much the sponge gives when the ball hits it. Butterfly's chart puts it simply: soft sponge absorbs more of the ball, suits a slower swing and suits beginners; hard sponge absorbs less, needs a fast swing and suits advanced players.

Butterfly's own figures show the range. Its Rozena, a rubber aimed at consistency, has a sponge hardness of 35. Tenergy 05 is 36. Dignics 09C, a tacky high-tension rubber, is 44. The Feint Long III, a defensive rubber, is 25. Higher numbers mean harder sponge.
## Why the numbers don't compare across brands

There is no single hardness scale. Butterfly says its sponge hardness is "measured by Butterfly's own standard", and other makers use their own methods. Chinese rubbers such as DHS's Hurricane 3 range are listed in degrees: the DHS Neo Hurricane 3 Hard, for example, is 40 degrees, and the range comes in several hardnesses either side of that. A Chinese rubber at 40 and a Japanese or European rubber at 40 are not necessarily the same firmness, so compare hardness within one brand's range, and read reviews or try a friend's bat before switching between brands. Our guide to [Chinese tacky and European tensor rubbers](/guide/tacky-vs-tensor-rubbers.html) explains why Chinese rubbers feel so different.
## Weight

Sponge adds weight. Butterfly publishes average weights for its rubbers measured at their thickest size, and its chart lists weight rising with thickness. If your bat feels heavy late in a session, a thinner sponge on one side is an easy way to lighten it. A blade's own weight is covered in [blades explained](/guide/table-tennis-blades-explained.html).
## What to choose at each stage

In your first months, use a ready-made bat with thin, soft sponge, and do not worry about the numbers. Once you play weekly and are learning to loop (a heavy topspin stroke), a custom bat with medium sponge, around 1.7mm to 1.9mm, on a medium-hard rubber is a sensible step. Move to 2.0mm or more and harder sponge only when your strokes are fast and consistent enough to use it, and change one thing at a time so you can tell what made the difference.
Next, read [rubbers explained](/guide/table-tennis-rubbers-explained.html) to choose the type of rubber that suits your game.
